cards.front: Can an enzyme make a thermodynamically impossible (uphill, unaided) reaction happen?
cards.back: No. An enzyme only makes a reaction that is already possible go fast, by lowering the energy barrier it has to cross.
cards.quote: An enzyme cannot make an impossible reaction happen. It can only make a possible one fast, by lowering the energy barrier the reaction has to cross.

cards.front: Picture substrate and product as two valleys with a ridge between them. Which part does an enzyme change, and which parts does it leave alone?
cards.back: It lowers only the ridge (ΔG‡). The valleys stay put, so ΔG, ΔG°′ and Keq do not change.
cards.why: The valleys set where the reaction goes; the ridge sets how fast it gets there.
cards.quote: An enzyme, like any catalyst, lowers only the ridge, never the two valleys.

cards.front: At 25 °C, every {{c1::5.7 kJ/mol}} taken off the activation barrier makes a reaction ten times faster.
cards.quote: every 5.7 kJ/mol taken off makes the reaction ten times faster

cards.front: About how much does OMP decarboxylase speed its reaction, and what is the uncatalyzed half-life?
cards.back: About 10¹⁷-fold. Uncatalyzed, the step has a half-life of 78 million years; with the enzyme it finishes in milliseconds.
cards.quote: Without it, that single step has a half-life of 78 million years, longer than the time since the dinosaurs vanished.

cards.front: What do a negative and a positive ΔG mean, and what are the two terms?
cards.back: Negative ΔG: releases free energy and can go forward on its own (exergonic, spontaneous). Positive ΔG: needs an energy input (endergonic).
cards.quote: A negative ΔG means the reaction releases free energy and can go forward on its own: it is exergonic, or spontaneous.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: Does "spontaneous" (negative ΔG) mean a reaction is fast?
cards.back: No. Spontaneous means downhill, not quick. Uncatalyzed OMP decarboxylation is downhill yet has a half-life of 78 million years.
cards.why: ΔG is thermodynamics (direction); speed is kinetics (the barrier).
cards.quote: Spontaneous means downhill, not quick, as uncatalyzed OMP decarboxylation shows.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: How does exothermic differ from exergonic?
cards.back: Exothermic is about heat (ΔH). Exergonic is about free energy (ΔG). A reaction can release free energy without releasing much heat.
cards.quote: exothermic is about heat (ΔH), and a reaction can release free energy without releasing much heat.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: How does ΔG differ from ΔG°′, and what equation links them?
cards.back: ΔG°′ is the standard reference value; ΔG is the value for the actual mixture. ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q, so ΔG depends on how much product and reactant are present.
cards.quote: ΔG°′ is the standard reference value, and ΔG the value for the mixture actually in the tube or the cell.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: Glucose + phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate has ΔG°′ = +13.8 kJ/mol. With 5 mM glucose, 1 mM phosphate and 0.001 mM G6P at 298 K (RT = 2.48 kJ/mol), what is ΔG, and is the reaction still uphill?
cards.why: Lowering product makes Q smaller and ΔG less positive, but not enough here to overcome +13.8.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol. In a red cell with ATP 2.25 mM, phosphate 1.65 mM and ADP raised to 2.5 mM, what is ΔG at 298 K (RT = 2.48 kJ/mol)?
cards.why: Tenfold more ADP raises Q tenfold, making ΔG about 5.7 kJ/mol less negative than the lesson's −52.
cards.quote: So ATP hydrolysis is the textbook exergonic reaction and direct G6P formation the textbook endergonic one, in standard conditions and in the cell.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: At equilibrium, what are ΔG and Q?
cards.back: ΔG = 0 and Q = Keq. As a reaction runs, Q moves toward Keq and ΔG creeps toward zero.
cards.quote: at equilibrium, going nowhere net, ΔG = 0 and Q = Keq.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: ΔG°′ = {{c1::−RT ln Keq}}, so ΔG°′ < 0 means Keq > 1.
cards.quote: The more negative ΔG°′, the larger Keq: ΔG°′ < 0 means Keq > 1, and ΔG°′ > 0 means Keq < 1.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: Why does a modest change in ΔG°′ shift the equilibrium constant a lot?
cards.back: Because ΔG°′ and Keq are related logarithmically: at 25 °C, each 5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG°′ is a factor of ten in Keq.
cards.quote: Because the relationship is logarithmic, a modest change in free energy moves the equilibrium a lot.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: A reaction has ΔG°′ = +11.4 kJ/mol at 298 K. Estimate Keq and say which side equilibrium favors.
cards.back: +11.4 kJ/mol is two factors of 5.7, so Keq ≈ 10⁻² (exactly, e^(−11,400 / (8.314 × 298)) = e^(−4.60) ≈ 0.010). Reactants are favored.
cards.quote: Quicker: every 5.7 kJ/mol is a factor of ten (the next section shows why), so 17 kJ/mol is about three.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: An enzyme that joins glucose directly to phosphate is added to a cell-like mix (5 mM glucose, 1 mM phosphate, 0.1 mM G6P; Q = 20). Does G6P pile up?
cards.back: No. ΔG is about +21 kJ/mol and the enzyme cannot change it. Keq is about 0.004, so Q = 20 is far past equilibrium; the enzyme only speeds net G6P breakdown.
cards.quote: This mix (Q = 20) is already far past it, so the enzyme would only speed the net reaction backward, breaking G6P down.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: Glucose + phosphate → G6P has ΔG°′ = +13.8 kJ/mol; ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol. Find ΔG°′ for hexokinase (glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP) and estimate its Keq at 298 K.
cards.why: Coupling adds ΔG°′ values of the combined reaction; ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq then converts to Keq.
cards.quote: Cells make G6P with hexokinase, which runs a different reaction: glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP, ΔG°′ = +13.8 − 30.5 = −16.7 kJ/mol, downhill.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: Hexokinase makes G6P downhill even though glucose + phosphate → G6P is uphill. Has the enzyme moved the equilibrium?
cards.back: No. That is coupling: hexokinase runs a different reaction that includes ATP's phosphate, so it is a change of reaction, not a moved equilibrium.
cards.quote: That is coupling: a change of reaction, not a moved equilibrium.
cards.section: Where a reaction ends up: ΔG, ΔG°′ and Q

cards.front: What is a transition state (X‡)?
cards.back: The structure at the very top of the energy pass: atoms with bonds half-broken and half-formed, neither substrate nor product, lasting femtoseconds.
cards.quote: atoms with bonds half-broken and half-formed, neither substrate nor product.
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: How does a transition state differ from an intermediate on a reaction energy diagram?
cards.back: A transition state is a peak, not a molecule you can isolate. An intermediate is a stable stop in a dip between two peaks.
cards.quote: a peak, not a molecule you can isolate (a stable stop between two peaks is an intermediate).
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: The height of the transition state above the substrate is the {{c1::activation energy, ΔG‡}}, and it sets the rate.
cards.quote: The height of that top above the substrate is the activation energy, ΔG‡, and it sets the rate.
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: An enzyme runs a step at 100 s⁻¹; the uncatalyzed step runs at 1 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. At 25 °C, what is the rate enhancement and about how much has the barrier been lowered?
cards.back: 100 ÷ (1 × 10⁻⁷) = 1 × 10⁹, nine factors of ten. Barrier lowered ≈ 9 × 5.7 ≈ 51 kJ/mol.
cards.why: At 25 °C each tenfold speed-up is 5.7 kJ/mol off the barrier.
cards.quote: Speed-up: 540 ÷ (2.9 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.9 × 10⁸, about 8.3 factors of ten.
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: An enzyme lowers the top of the energy ridge for substrate → product. What happens to the barrier for the reverse reaction, and to Keq?
cards.back: The reverse barrier falls too. From the fixed free substrate and free product, both trips cross the same lowered top, so both speed up by the same factor and Keq is unchanged.
cards.quote: so forward and reverse speed up by the same factor and their ratio, Keq, does not change.
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: Two identical reaction mixes start far from equilibrium; one gets an enzyme. Compare their final concentrations and how long each takes to reach them.
cards.back: Same final concentrations; the enzyme mix gets there sooner.
cards.why: An enzyme cannot change ΔG, ΔG°′ or Keq; it only speeds the approach.
cards.quote: An enzyme cannot change ΔG, ΔG°′, or Keq; it reaches the same equilibrium sooner.
cards.section: How fast it gets there: the height of the hill

cards.front: How does an enzyme's active site lower the activation barrier?
cards.back: It fits the distorted transition state better than the substrate. The extra binding energy released on the transition state, beyond what goes to the substrate, comes off the climb.
cards.quote: Binding releases energy (binding energy), and the extra that goes to the transition state, beyond what goes to the substrate, comes off the climb from the bound substrate.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: Speed-up from the bound substrate: kcat / kuncat = {{c1::Kd(substrate) / Kd(transition state)}}.
cards.back: The lower the Kd, the tighter the grip.
cards.quote: kcat / kuncat = Kd(substrate) / Kd(transition state), where kcat is the rate of the step from the bound substrate and kuncat the rate with no enzyme.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: A designed enzyme holds its substrate exactly as tightly as it holds the transition state. How much faster is the step once the substrate is bound?
cards.back: Not faster at all. The bound substrate and the top drop by the same amount, so the climb from the bound substrate is as high as before.
cards.quote: The bound substrate and the top drop by the same amount, so the climb from the bound substrate is as high as before.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: An enzyme speeds a step 10⁹-fold from the bound substrate. A mutation makes it bind substrate 100-fold more tightly but leaves its grip on the transition state unchanged. At 25 °C, what is the new speed-up, and how much higher is the climb from the bound substrate?
cards.back: The Kd ratio falls 100-fold, so the speed-up becomes 10⁷. Two factors of ten lost: 2 × 5.7 ≈ 11.4 kJ/mol higher climb.
cards.why: kcat / kuncat = Kd(substrate) / Kd(transition state); only the numerator changed.
cards.quote: Worse, tightening the substrate's grip alone shrinks that speed-up
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: Why do enzymes hold substrates only moderately but transition states extremely tightly?
cards.back: Rate depends on the extra grip on the transition state relative to the substrate. Tighter substrate binding alone shrinks that difference and slows catalysis when the enzyme is saturated.
cards.quote: Enzymes hold substrates moderately and transition states extremely tightly.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: Besides binding the transition state, name the other catalytic tools enzymes use.
cards.back: Holding reacting groups close and lined up, acid-base catalysis (passing protons), covalent catalysis (brief covalent bonds with substrate), and metal ions.
cards.quote: pass protons to and from the substrate (acid-base catalysis), form brief covalent bonds with it (covalent catalysis), and use metal ions.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: Why does the simple transition-state grip rule become less direct for covalent catalysis?
cards.back: Covalent catalysis changes the transition state itself, so the rule then compares two different transition states (catalyzed and uncatalyzed).
cards.quote: covalent catalysis in particular changes the transition state itself, so the simple rule then compares two different transition states.
cards.section: How an enzyme lowers the top: grip the transition state

cards.front: Proline racemase passes through a planar transition state. Chemists compared its binding of L-proline with a stable flat look-alike, pyrrole-2-carboxylate. What did they find, and what does it show?
cards.back: The flat analog bound with Kd 0.022 mM versus 3.6 mM for L-proline, about 160 times tighter. The active site is built to fit the transition state, not the substrate.
cards.quote: Chemists made pyrrole-2-carboxylate, a stable flat look-alike the enzyme cannot turn over.
cards.section: The evidence: transition-state analogs bind tighter

cards.front: Proline racemase binds a transition-state analog with Kd 0.022 mM and its substrate with Kd 3.6 mM. Find the fold-tighter binding and convert it to kJ/mol at 25 °C.
cards.quote: 160-fold is about 2.2 factors of ten, or 12.6 kJ/mol
cards.section: The evidence: transition-state analogs bind tighter

cards.front: The proline racemase analog captures only about 12.6 kJ/mol of extra binding, while enzymes like those in the lesson lower barriers by 47 to 97 kJ/mol. Does this undercut the transition-state binding explanation?
cards.back: No. An analog is an imperfect mimic of so fleeting a structure, so it captures only part of the grip. Read 160-fold as a down payment, not the full account.
cards.quote: An analog is an imperfect mimic of so fleeting a structure, so it captures only part of the grip
cards.section: The evidence: transition-state analogs bind tighter

cards.front: Why can a rigid lock-and-key active site not explain catalysis?
cards.back: A rigid lock built for the substrate would bind the substrate most tightly. Enzymes do not: their sites fit the transition state best.
cards.quote: But a rigid lock built for the substrate would bind the substrate most tightly, and enzymes don't
cards.section: A separate question: does the active site change shape?

cards.front: How does induced fit differ from conformational selection?
cards.back: Induced fit: substrate binding changes the enzyme's shape and brings catalytic groups into line. Conformational selection: the enzyme already shifts between shapes, and the substrate picks the one that fits. Real enzymes often mix both.
cards.quote: substrate binding changes the enzyme's shape and brings its catalytic groups into line.
cards.section: A separate question: does the active site change shape?

cards.front: A student says induced fit replaces the idea that enzymes bind the transition state tightly. Is that right?
cards.back: No. They answer different questions: transition-state complementarity is about what the site fits best; induced fit is about whether the site changes shape. An enzyme can do both.
cards.quote: What the active site fits best and whether it changes shape are different questions.
cards.section: A separate question: does the active site change shape?

cards.front: A chemist designs a stable molecule shaped like an enzyme's transition state that the enzyme cannot turn over. Predict how it binds relative to the substrate and its effect on activity.
cards.back: It binds the active site more tightly than the substrate does (the lesson's analog: 160-fold) and, since the enzyme cannot turn it over, can shut the enzyme down.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the active site is most complementary to the transition state.
cards.quote: Drugs shaped like a transition state, as in the film's last panel, exploit the same logic: they bind the active site far more tightly than the substrate does.
cards.section: Tight binding as a drug strategy

cards.front: What enzyme do statins block, and how do they inhibit it?
cards.back: HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. They are competitive inhibitors, not true transition-state analogs: they mimic the HMG part and bind with nanomolar affinity.
cards.quote: They block HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
cards.section: Tight binding as a drug strategy

cards.front: A patient starts a statin. Predict the liver's handling of LDL cholesterol and the effect on blood cholesterol.
cards.back: The liver pulls more LDL cholesterol out of the blood, so blood cholesterol falls.
cards.why: Slowing the liver's own cholesterol synthesis drives it to take up more from the blood.
cards.quote: Slowing the pathway makes the liver pull more LDL cholesterol out of the blood, lowering blood cholesterol as intended.
cards.section: Tight binding as a drug strategy

cards.front: Are all enzymes proteins? Give the key counterexample.
cards.back: No. Some enzymes are RNA (ribozymes); the ribosome, which builds every protein, is one.
cards.quote: some enzymes are RNA (ribozymes), and the ribosome that builds every protein in your body is itself one.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: Name the seven EC enzyme classes and what each does.
cards.back: Oxidoreductases (move electrons), transferases (move a group), hydrolases (break a bond with water), lyases (add/remove groups across a double bond), isomerases (rearrange), ligases (join two molecules, usually with ATP), translocases (move across membranes).
cards.quote: There are seven official classes, sorted by the chemistry they do.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: Hexokinase moves a phosphate group from ATP onto glucose. Which EC class is it, and what is the first digit of its EC number?
cards.back: A transferase; first digit 2 (EC 2.7.1.1).
cards.why: It moves a chemical group from one molecule to another; the EC number's first digit is the class.
cards.quote: Each enzyme gets a four-part EC number whose first digit is its class: hexokinase, a transferase, is EC 2.7.1.1.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: Fumarase adds a water molecule across the double bond of fumarate, leaving one molecule. It uses water. Is it a hydrolase?
cards.back: No, a lyase. A hydrolase uses water to cut one molecule into two; fumarase adds water across a double bond.
cards.why: Classify by what happens to the bonds, not by whether water appears.
cards.quote: A hydrolase uses water to cut one molecule into two; fumarase adds water across a double bond and leaves one molecule.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: What are the two kinds of cofactor? Give an example of each.
cards.back: A coenzyme: organic, usually vitamin-derived (niacin becomes NAD⁺; thiamine becomes TPP). A metal ion: inorganic (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺).
cards.quote: A coenzyme is an organic molecule, usually derived from a vitamin (niacin becomes NAD⁺; thiamine becomes TPP).
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: What is a prosthetic group, and what is the classic example?
cards.back: A cofactor, organic or metal, that binds tightly and permanently rather than coming and going. Classic example: the heme in catalase.
cards.quote: the heme buried in catalase, an organic ring holding an iron ion, is the classic example.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: A dehydrogenase loses all activity when its NAD⁺ is removed and regains it when NAD⁺ is added back. Name the inactive protein, the active complex, and the kind of cofactor NAD⁺ is.
cards.back: Inactive protein: apoenzyme. Active complex: holoenzyme. NAD⁺ is a coenzyme (organic, vitamin-derived cofactor).
cards.why: Apo means away; holo means whole.
cards.quote: an enzyme missing its cofactor is an apoenzyme and it does not work; the assembled, working complex is the holoenzyme.
cards.section: Naming enzymes and their helpers

cards.front: What does the Haldane relation state, and what does it imply about enzymes and equilibrium?
cards.back: (kcat/KM) forward over (kcat/KM) reverse equals Keq. The free-end speed-up is equal forward and reverse, so no enzyme can move the equilibrium.
cards.quote: (kcat/KM) forward over (kcat/KM) reverse equals Keq (the Haldane relation), which is why no enzyme can move the equilibrium.
cards.section: The bookkeeping behind the rule

cards.front: Triosephosphate isomerase is nearly limited by how fast substrate diffuses in. An engineer adds contacts that grip its chemical transition state more tightly. Predict the effect on overall rate.
cards.back: Little or no gain. Once substrate diffusion nearly limits the rate, as it nearly does for this enzyme, extra grip on the chemical transition state no longer helps.
cards.why: The grip rule applies to the highest barrier; here that is nearly diffusion, not chemistry.
cards.quote: Once an enzyme is limited by how fast substrate diffuses in, as triosephosphate isomerase nearly is, extra grip on the chemical transition state no longer helps.
cards.section: The bookkeeping behind the rule

cards.front: Is CoQ10 depletion the proven cause of muscle symptoms on statins?
cards.back: No. It is one proposed explanation. CoQ10 supplements have not reliably helped, and in blinded trials most aches on statins also occur on placebo.
cards.quote: in blinded trials most muscle aches reported on statins also occur on placebo
cards.section: Statins and muscle symptoms
